item.content:encoded:
The Toronto Blue Jays have endured a highly disappointing season after winning the American League last year.
The Blue Jays have now officially been eliminated from MLB postseason contention after being swept by the Baltimore Orioles earlier this week. The team struggled to find consistent production throughout the season, and now sits in last place in the AL East at 77-82.
One of the biggest disappointments during an overall frustrating season has been first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
The six-time All-Star signed a 14-year, $500 million extension with Toronto in April of 2025 and followed it with an excellent season and a trip to the World Series. However, in the 2026 season, he has seen a steep drop-off in production.
A season to forget
Sep 18, 2026; Arlington, Texas, USA; Toronto Blue Jays first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. (27) walks to the dugout after the end of the fifth inning against the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field. Mandatory Credit: Raymond Carlin III-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
Guerrero is slashing .263/.335/.360 with just nine home runs and 56 RBIs in 142 games. His .695 OPS is the lowest mark of his career. With Toronto's season effectively over, Guerrero's recent comments surrounding his contract were met with a flurry of scrutiny.
In a conversation with Veronica Batista, Guerrero said in Spanish, "The money they gave me wasn't for what I'm going to do. It was for what I already did. They didn't pay me because I'm going to hit 40 every year. They paid me for what I already accomplished."
Given his struggles this season, fans criticized the comments. Guerrero later stood by his remarks, making it clear he is not looking to avoid responsibility.
Guerrero has since received support from Hall of Fame pitcher Pedro Martínez, who is also Guerrero's godfather. Martínez defended Guerrero, stating he was misunderstood and was not intending to excuse his current performance.
Martínez pushes back
Phillip Feliz spoke with Martínez, who said, "He was misinterpreted. What he meant is that contract came from what he's already done, and what he can still do. That's a young man talking. He just didn't explain himself the right way."
Pedro Martínez, Vladdy's godfather, on the contract comments:
"He was misinterpreted. What he meant is that contract came from what he's already done, and what he can still do. That's a young man talking. He just didn't explain himself the right way." pic.twitter.com/W0wXvrGh5y
— Master Flip | Phillip Feliz 🇩🇴 (@Masterflip_) September 25, 2026
Guerrero's comments may have sounded poorly timed given his and the team's struggles this season. However, Martínez wants critics to know that the contract rewarded what Guerrero had already established while also reflecting the belief that he can still produce at a high level moving forward.
For Guerrero, a rebound at the plate next season will be the clearest way to move past this controversy. With 13 seasons left on his deal, he has plenty of time to show Blue Jays fans that he can live up to the expectations of his extension.

The Seattle Mariners have had a rough 2026 season. After coming one win shy of the World Series a year ago, they've failed to make the postseason despite the AL West leader having a record under .500 with three games to go.
This Mariners season is one of the worst in recent years due to the expectations coming into the season. A lot of people are to blame, but one of the main reasons why things fell apart is thanks to Cal Raleigh.
Jayson Stark of The Athletic named Raleigh the American League's "LVP" or "Least Valuable Player." Instead of Vladimir Guerrero Jr. earning this label for his poor 2026 season, Raleigh is the LVP of the season for a few key reasons.
Why Cal Raleigh earned LVP award over Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
"The Mariners' catcher has gone from MVP runner-up, 60-homer machine and heartbeat of a team that was eight outs from the World Series to... eh, hoo boy," Stark writes. "The Big Dumper has been worth 1.1 WAR all season, according to Baseball Reference..."
Raleigh's drop-off this season isn't limited to just some struggles to accumulate bWAR. There is so much else that's gone wrong for the Mariners catcher.
"But would that alone have been enough to push Raleigh 'ahead' of Vladdy in this LVP derby? It would not," Stark writes. "To pull that off would have taken one of the steepest drop-offs, from one season to the next, in baseball history. Unfortunately for Raleigh, that's what he's enduring."
Raleigh has gone from 60 homers to 23 with three games to go. That's the biggest drop-off of all-time for a 60-homer hitter, according to Stark.
Regarding his 1.1 bWAR, Stark shared, "And if you're wondering how many top-two MVP finishers have ever gone from at least 7.0 that year to under 2. 0the next, that would be none -- until now."
Raleigh's drop-off in homers and bWAR is something baseball has never seen before. But it's so much more than just those two poor statistics.
He posted a slash line of .247/.359/.589 last season. In 2026, his average dropped 68 points, his on-base percentage 63 points, and his slugging percentage an astounding 220 points with three games to go.
Those numbers will look different by the end of the season, but those are some truly terrible drop-offs, even if he were to get hot in these final three games of 2026.
Going from a 169 OPS+ to a 92 OPS+, and a .948 OPS to a .663 OPS, is an all-time fall-off for any player in MLB history.
All of that is exceptionally terrible production, but considering Guerrero has just nine homers this season with a .695 OPS and a 92 OPS+, he's not the "LVP" this season due to the sheer drop-off from Raleigh in 2025 to 2026.
It's not just the drop-off for Raleigh that's playing a role here either. The Blue Jays had a rough 2026 season, but they at least played better than Seattle did this year.
Raleigh is the "LVP" of the American League in 2026 thanks to the record-breaking drop-off he's had from 2025 to 2026.
While he might not be the worst player in the AL, his production in 2026 is far below what was expected of him this season and is more than deserving of the "Least Valuable Player" label this year.

Vladimir Guerrero Jr.’s not wrong, but he’s also not right
Photo credit: Cary Edmondson-Imagn Images
The Toronto Blue Jays’ offseason hasn’t even begun, but the club is already the talk of baseball thanks to the face of their franchise, Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
He may have put his foot in his mouth when his comments made the rounds earlier this week after an interview with podcaster Veronica Batista. Guerrero seemed to express remorse about his disappointing season, but his remarks weren’t perceived that way by some fans.
First of all, the timing of this interview could not have been worse. The video came out the day the Blue Jays were eliminated from postseason contention. It’s almost as if it were planned that way for maximum exposure and general outrage.
Had this interview taken place earlier this season, or during the offseason, there would be a different tenor about it. But with a lot of vitriol among the Blue Jays fan base, these comments have not sat well among Jays devotees.
There are some areas where he’s right and some areas where he’s wrong. The comment that drew the most ire was Guerrero saying, “They didn’t pay me because I’m going to hit 40 every year. They paid me for what I already accomplished.”
Is this Vladdy saying the quiet part out loud, or is there credence to what he said?
Professional baseball players are criminally underpaid at the beginning of their careers. To earn the league minimum through the first three years of their Major League journey, followed by three years of arbitration (four if you’re lucky to reach Super Two status), is a big reason many teams can afford to keep their productive players.
The value that Guerrero provided at the beginning of his career far exceeded what he was paid before he signed his monster contract. According to FanGraphs’ Value metric, Vladdy provided $164 million in value through his first seven seasons in the big leagues while earning $72.5 million.
Anyone aside from MLB owners would agree the salary arbitration model is broken, so it’s easy to see why Guerrero feels like his $500 million contract is a delayed payment for his early-career production. Surely, there are many MLB players who are silently yelling “PREACH” after hearing what Guerrero said.
In that moment, Vlad was acting as an advocate for his fellow players. Given that the players and owners are hurtling toward a lockout on December 2, his stance was understandable. He is one of the faces of Major League Baseball, so as Vlad goes, so too does the rest of the league.
But that’s not how modern-day contracts work. Nine-figure deals paying for past production may be a Pollyanna perspective held by some professional athletes, but those contracts bank on future production more than the past. As much as MLB executives might spin it to the players as a thank you for services tendered, it’s not totally accurate.
Guerrero should be given some grace, as not everything he said in the video (and the follow-up comments) was flame-worthy. In a way, he admitted the pressure of the $500 million contract is weighing on him, which is to be expected for any 27-year-old handed the keys to the Blue Jays for the next 13 years.
Although Guerrero surely meant no harm during that interview, he had to have known his comments would be unnerving to folks in Toronto. The optics are bad, and this is a PR blunder. At the very least, his handlers should’ve had a better grasp on the temperature of the Blue Jays fan base and asked to delay the release of the interview, rather than have it drop at the worst possible moment.
After the disappointing season Vlad had, some fans wanted their pound of flesh, and anything less than a full admission of ineptitude wouldn’t suffice. When a player carries a team like Guerrero did in the postseason last year and then virtually disappears the following season, people want answers.
Vlad didn’t have an answer that made anyone feel better about how 2026 went down, which may be the underlying reason for all this venom in the first place. Guerrero can’t just “aw shucks” a single-digit home run total and sub-.700 OPS season away, but for baseball players, compartmentalizing failure is what makes them successful.
Had Vladdy missed significant time this season due to injuries, there would be a little more tolerance for his underperformance. The fact that he played 140+ games this year, claiming to not be injured, almost makes it worse because his regression can’t be blamed on an injury.
I don’t believe the Blue Jays have buyer’s remorse already, but this is the risk you run plunking a half-billion dollars into one player. If they carry the team on their back, they’re the GOAT. If they fail, they’re the goat.
It’s an apples-to-oranges situation, but the Boston Red Sox ran Rafael Devers out of town after giving him the keys to Beantown. A few years after inking a 10-year, $331 million extension, the fracture between Devers and the Red Sox front office grew so wide that he was traded to the San Francisco Giants.
I’m not saying the same fate befalls Toronto’s golden child, but we’re already starting to witness the side effects of tying up so much money in one player. The fan base hasn’t turned on Guerrero, but this could start to get ugly if he fails to turn things around in 2027.
2026 will not only be remembered as a golden opportunity missed by the Blue Jays but also by Vladdy himself. Guerrero wasn’t wrong with many of the things he said, but he also wasn’t right. The timing was atrocious, but hey, isn’t that typical of Toronto sports?

TORONTO – Baseball is full of long days and short years, which is how it can simultaneously feel like George Springer’s been with the Toronto Blue Jays forever and that the six seasons in his then-club-record $150-million free-agent contract have flown by.
So much has happened since he signed that fateful agreement Jan. 23, 2021, while the federal government’s pandemic restrictions that locked the club out of its home for a season-and-a-half were still in place.
Despite 91 wins, the Blue Jays missed the playoffs by one measly game in that vagabond three-home-sites ’21 season, before jarring wild-card exits followed in each of the next two years.
As a three-stage renovation completely transformed the Rogers Centre, a train-wreck 2024 was chased by the exhilarating run to — and subsequent heartbreak of — the 2025 World Series, the slugger delivering a franchise-pantheon Game 7 ALCS homer along the way.
He earned an all-star selection and a Silver Slugger, poured into his teammates, set a standard in the clubhouse, became a symbol of the club’s re-emergence as a legitimate player in the free-agent market and is so ingrained within the organization’s fabric that his seven preceding seasons with the Houston Astros feel more like fever dream than reality.
Yet suddenly, the end is nigh, with three games versus the visiting Cincinnati Reds beginning Friday night (7 p.m. ET / 4 p.m. PT, Sportsnet, Sportsnet+) all that remains of those six years, and perhaps in his career, too.
“It’s emotional to think about it,” Springer said Wednesday in a quiet corner of the visitors' clubhouse at Camden Yards, after an Orioles doubleheader sweep eliminated the Blue Jays from the wild-card chase. “Very, very grateful to our fans, this team, this organization. Obviously this is not the way that we all wanted it to end. But if it is, I'm going to do my best to embrace being back home for one last time and making sure that I do anything I can to reciprocate to the fans.”
Springer is coy about the future beyond that, although some close to him expect that he will retire once all is said and done. At 37, having willed his way through far more ailments than he will acknowledge, having won one World Series, tainted as it may be by the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal, and come within inches of another, with 308 homers and a career OPS of .823 over 13 seasons, his resume is substantial.
His final season — .251/.323/.407 with 15 homers and 54 RBIs — would surely look different if a foul tip hadn’t fractured his left big toe May 11 and forced him to play compromised for weeks once he returned.
In 58 games since the all-star break, though, he’s posted an .800 OPS with six homers and 32 RBIs, demonstrating that even through subsequent shoulder issues, he can still do damage. Combined with his veteran leadership and experience, there is sure to be a market for him during the off-season, if he wants to continue playing.
Does he?
“I don't know,” he replied. “I love this organization. I loved being a Blue Jay. I've loved every single bit of being here. I haven't really gotten that far yet. I've kind of taken every day with these guys in stride.”
As he usually does, Springer shrugged off the toll his aggressive style has taken on him physically and insisted that won’t tip the scales in his decision-making.
“If my mind can say it, then my body can do it – my body can do whatever I tell it to do, hopefully,” he said. “But I'll cross that road once I get to it. We've still got to get through these next three and then we'll go into the off-season and I'll see what happens.”
More of a factor will be the needs of his family as Springer and wife Charlise have three sons aged five, three and three-months-old. The two older boys have been clubhouse staples this season, often walking around with either a bat or a glove in hand, following their dad through each stage of his pre-game. During a recent homestand, they each took a round of batting practice on the field once the Blue Jays were done and ran the bases after.
“It's hard to be away from them and to miss things,” said Springer. “I want to be able to give them hugs and say, I love you in person. It's been a long year for me off the field. But those are my kids and I love them. I'll sit down with my wife at the end of this year and we'll discuss whatever's going to happen. But I love my family and if that requires me to be with them, I'll be with them.”
In some ways that would be a natural transition, given the way Springer’s grown into a father-figure type during his time with the Blue Jays.
During one down stretch in May, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. pointed out that “George is my advice guy,” and praised Springer for telling him to “go out there and be yourself, laughing, joking” because “sometimes you put too much pressure and then sometimes you change your body language, so he always tells us to go out there and have fun.”
Myles Straw, who also played with Springer in Houston, recently praised the way he brought calmness and energy through games of increasing leverage, saying, “I've seen George do it for years now … Even in the playoffs, it's like Game 1 of the season for George.”
Manager John Schneider, who’s praised Springer in so many ways over the years, pointed out last month how important his guidance was through this summer’s trade deadline, when the Blue Jays traded away Kevin Gausman, Daulton Varsho and Jeff Hoffman but still crawled back into contention.
“That's part of the reason we signed him when we did, he's remarkably aware of how things can change and he doesn't panic,” said Schneider. “That rubs off on everyone and his will to say like, ‘Hey, I'm going to do whatever it takes to win today,’ has rubbed off on some guys. He's been great. He's still having fun and he's still affecting people around him.”
During his 3.5 seasons with the Blue Jays, Varsho grew especially close to Springer, who’d regularly walk through the clubhouse calling, “Daulton,” when he couldn’t find the centre-fielder.
“I’m going to cherish every moment that we've had together because he's taught me a lot about myself, just what it means to be a leader and how to do it in the right way,” Varsho said Aug. 1. “He's a lead-by-example guy and he'll use his voice every once in a while when he needs to. It's a pretty spectacular career he's had. Obviously I keep talking to him, I want him to keep playing, but obviously for him it's his choice and his family's choice. But he's had a hell of a career and it's always been enjoyable for me to play alongside him.”
All combined, it’s a sizable legacy Springer has carved out with the Blue Jays, who signed him to push the franchise to the next level and saw him do precisely that. At the time of his 2021 signing, president and CEO Mark Shapiro said, “there's no limit to what this market can be, it's a behemoth and we're going to continue to get better and continue to add the players and keep the players that we have necessary to be a championship team year-in, year-out.”
In that way, the Blue Jays achieved what they envisioned — save for the championship — when they invested in Springer six years ago.
Asked if he’s accomplished all he wanted with Toronto, minus the title, Springer replied, “I don't know. I hope so.”
“I’d hope that over the last six years, I've been able to show the fans and this organization that I love them and I'll play as hard as I can every single day with whatever I've got,” he continued. “At the end of the day, the goal was to win the World Series and we came an eyelash shy. But to see all the progress that we made as organization and a team, just to be standing on that field in Game 7 was a dream come true for me. So yeah, I'd love to be the last team standing, but this has been a hell of a six years.”
One series left. Time sure does fly.

Most of baseball’s awards races are formalities this year. The favorites are clear, and deservedly so. Pete Crow-Armstrong is having one of the greatest seasons of the 21st century. Jacob Misiorowski is a closer throwing starter innings. Bobby Witt Jr. has been terrific, but Yordan Alvarez is unsolvable. Cam Schlittler has more fastballs than batters have answers. Kevin McGonigle is a phenom. But I’m most interested in the sixth major race: National League Rookie of the Year. The gambling odds would tell you that it too is settled, with Sal Stewart the prohibitive favorite. But if I had a vote this year, I’d cast it for JJ Wetherholt, and I want to explain myself because I think this race provides a fascinating look into old school versus new school baseball statistics, and how both have blind spots.
Before we get into my argument, let’s get a few disclaimers out of the way. I am not voting for NL Rookie of the Year. I’m not a member of the BBWAA, even. I haven’t placed any wagers on NL ROY, or on any awards, or on anything even peripherally related to this. I was a Cardinals fan before I started working in baseball, but that has faded away. I have a lot of fond memories of Ozzie Smith, but I’m a fan of the sport now, not a team, and I’ve watched more Reds games than Cardinals games this year because I love watching Elly De La Cruz play. No one in the world is truly unbiased, but I don’t have a horse in this race in any meaningful way.
With that out of the way, let’s get down to brass tacks. The two leading candidates for the award are Stewart and Wetherholt, with Carson Benge a distant-enough third according to the odds that I’m largely leaving him out of the discussion, though he’ll make some cameos. Stewart’s résumé revolves around his thunderous bat. He’s batting .266/.333/.465, with 32 homers and a gaudy 110 RBI. Even in an offense-friendly home park, that’s good for a 115 wRC+, 15th-best among qualifying first basemen, and of course the RBI total is better than that. He’s played so-so defense at first – not that I care much about that in award voting – and has accrued 2.2 WAR per our calculation of the statistic.
If Stewart’s calling card is his power, Wetherholt’s is his lack of weaknesses. He’s hitting .244/.343/.365, good for a 103 wRC+, with 17 homers despite playing his home games in cavernous Busch Stadium. He walks a ton and rarely strikes out. He’s a plus baserunner and an elite defender at second base, where he’s the favorite for a Gold Glove and is sure to draw strong consideration in my Fielding Bible voting. Between his ability to get on base, his baserunning, his defense, and the fact that WAR values second basemen more highly than first basemen for the same batting line, we have him at 4.5 WAR, the best mark among NL rookies. Benge is second on that list at 3.7 WAR; he’s been a better hitter than Wetherholt and a better defender than Stewart.
Great – now let’s throw WAR out the window. When I tell you that one of these players has nearly double the WAR of the other and that the one with the lower WAR total is a favorite to win the award, that should tell you that “but look at the WAR” isn’t a good argument. I’ll mention the building blocks of WAR again in this article, because the building blocks of WAR are “playing baseball” more or less, but the headline number? Banished to the shadow realm.
While “rookie” is exceedingly well defined for the purposes of this award, “of the year” has no obvious qualifications. It’s simply the best rookie-eligible player in each voter’s estimation. That leaves the field wide open, and it means that many different interpretations have merit. My own interpretation is that the award should go to the best-performing rookie, with their expected future production used sparingly as a tiebreaker. If a voter wanted to instead vote for the rookie they thought had the brightest future, though, I wouldn’t argue with them – that’s as much a rookie of the year as my version.
This year, my interpretation means that I need to compare Stewart’s power to Wetherholt’s all-around game. And like I mentioned, we won’t be using WAR to make the decision for us. It’s clearly true that being better at defense is important, and it’s also clearly true that if two players had the same batting line, you’d prefer an average-fielding shortstop over a DH. But I don’t think it’s reasonable to say that Wetherholt was nearly three wins more valuable than Stewart by virtue of position and defense. That’s just too many wins for me to take as gospel. Defensive statistics are noisy. Positional adjustments aren’t set in stone. We’re going to go component-by-component instead.
It’s important to give Stewart appropriate credit for his run production ability, and I don’t think that wRC+ fully captures it. That statistic measures every single plate appearance in a neutral context. That’s very useful for figuring out the future, because hitters don’t control the context they bat in, but it’s less useful for saying how much a hitter helped his team win in the games they actually played.
I don’t think RBI numbers are a very good way of capturing that either, though. It’s immediately obvious that team context has a ton to do with RBI totals. A hitter who batted with the bases loaded every time would have a ludicrous RBI total even if he was terrible; a hitter who always came up with the bases empty could be peak Ted Williams and still put up paltry RBI numbers. Now, those two scenarios aren’t realistic. But leadoff hitters bat with runners on base far less often than cleanup hitters. Teams with poor offenses give their hitters fewer opportunities to drive a run home. Like many statistics, RBI totals reflect a blend of skill, opportunity, and chance – round ball and round bat, as they always say.
Fortunately, there’s a statistic that accounts for opportunity: the clumsily-named RE24. That name sounds like an experimental drug from a sci-fi movie, but it’s actually a straightforward idea. Take the situation before a hitter comes to the plate. Then take the situation after they finish batting, accounting for runs scored, runners advanced, and whether or not they made an out. Turn it all into run expectancy, and give them credit (or assign them blame) for the difference in run-scoring expectation before and after their at-bat.
To put this in more concrete terms, consider a plate appearance that starts with a runner on third and one out. A sacrifice fly moves the expected runs scored in that inning from 0.86 to 1.1, crediting the hitter with 0.24 runs of value. A strikeout drops the expected runs scored that inning from 0.86 to 0.32, docking the hitter 0.54 runs. Or consider a runner on third with two outs. A single moves run scoring expectations from 0.32 to 1.21, a gain of 0.89 runs. A walk, on the other hand, only bumps the run expectancy from 0.32 to 0.48, a gain of 0.16 runs. Want a statistic that says a single is better than a walk when you can drive in a run, or that strikeouts with runners in scoring position are bad? RE24 does the trick. It also handles the other side of the equation well. With the bases empty, a walk really is as good as a single, and RE24 agrees.
By considering the state when a hitter comes to the plate, RE24 accounts for opportunity. All you can do as a hitter is play the hand you’re dealt. RE24 measures “the hand you’re dealt” in a slightly smarter way than just ignoring it completely. I don’t think it’s controversial to say that situational hitting – changing your approach based on the game situation – is a real thing that batters do. RE24 sets the incentives right; it gives you credit for doing the thing that makes your team score the most runs, and by construction “the thing that makes your team score the most runs” is different in different situations.
RE24 thinks Stewart is pretty dang good. It has him 20.3 runs above average this year. In other words, a perfectly league average batter hitting in his spot would have cost the Reds 20-ish runs in one way or another – fewer homers, more strikeouts in big spots, fewer baserunners to open innings, the whole gamut of ways that Stewart has added value this season. Those RBIs are a big part of it. He’s second on his team in RE24 behind De La Cruz (sure, checks out), and second only to TJ Rumfield, who gets to play in Colorado, among qualifying NL rookies. Given that RE24 doesn’t adjust for park, I’m comfortable saying that no NL rookie did more with their bat than Stewart.
Of course, Wetherholt was no slouch offensively either. While Stewart batted second, third, and fourth and cashed in runners in front of him, Wetherholt led off in every game he played this year. His OBP-heavy game is a great fit for how often he came up with the bases empty; when there are no runners to advance, a walk is as good as a hit, and his double-digit walk rate is perfect in that spot. RE24 gives Wetherholt credit for 10.2 runs above average. (Benge is marginally ahead of Wetherholt here at 11.3 runs.)
That’s one estimate of the gap in value between Stewart’s bat and Wetherholt’s bat – 10 to 11 runs. If you’re interested in another, there’s Win Probability Added. Think RE24, but instead of measuring how many runs are likely to score, WPA measures how likely the batting team is to win before and after the plate appearance. No one cares if you hit a grand slam in a 23-3 blowout. A two-run single, down a run in the ninth, is far more valuable to a team’s chances of winning. Why not account for that in our statistics?
WPA thinks that Stewart has added about 1.4 wins to the Reds’ total, as compared to a league average hitter, based on what he’s done in the situations he’s faced. That’s pretty good! Only five rookie hitters in all of baseball have a better mark, and four of them play in the American League. But the fifth member of that group is Wetherholt, who checks in at 1.99 WPA. Though he’s been a worse hitter than Stewart overall, his worst performances have come when there are no stakes. In low-leverage situations, he’s batting a putrid .228/.340/.296, 12% below average. The rest of the time, he’s been 14% above average offensively. In other words, he concentrated his best performances when it mattered most. Stewart, on the other hand, has been steady: very good in high leverage, good in medium leverage, good in low leverage. Benge looks worse by WPA; thanks to some rough performances in big spots, he only gets credit for 0.5 wins.
I don’t think that WPA is a fair measure for evaluating the best rookie, so I would not consider it if I were voting. I mentioned it just in case a voter reading this wanted to take clutchness into account. There’s no evidence that it’s a skill. There’s no evidence that this means Wetherholt will continue to play his best when it matters most. But if you want to give the award to the hitter whose offense was worth the most expected wins at the moment it happened, that would surprisingly be Wetherholt.
I’m much more aligned with RE24’s accounting of the world for this award. I love WPA for awards like MVP that care about “valuable” rather than “best,” and I’m sure I’ll get an article out of that in the long winter we have ahead. I concur that Stewart is a better hitter than Wetherholt, and I think 12 runs is a perfectly reasonable estimate for how much better. He’s been very good in the role the Reds deployed him in, cashing in baserunners. Wetherholt has been good at getting on base to set the table, but Stewart’s bat is clearly more valuable.
One last point on the RBI front: Stewart’s RBI total is impressive, of course, and I don’t think “RBIs don’t matter” is a reasonable dismissal of that. It’s certainly not a way to win an argument. Runs win games, after all. But even if you care a lot about RBIs, you have to adjust them for context. Stewart was 10th in the majors this year when it came to having runners on base when he batted. The top 10 averaged 95 RBI. He did better than that average, but it’s not like his opportunity set didn’t matter. When you bat with so many dudes aboard, you’re going to drive some of them home. We care about how much better he did in the situations he was put into, and 15 extra RBI is no joke, nor are the 21 runs above average that RE24 credits him with. But you can’t just say 110 RBI with no context, because the Reds did a really good job of setting Stewart up with runners on base.
Next, let’s consider baserunning. Wetherholt has stolen 14 bases. Stewart has stolen 15. But Wetherholt is quite efficient, with only one time caught stealing, while Stewart has been gunned down six times. That isn’t good considering that you need to run a 75%-ish success rate on steals to break even. Stewart’s aggression has cost the Reds about half a run compared to just not attempting to steal, while Wetherholt’s attempts have added about 1.5 runs to St. Louis’ ledger.
Excluding steals, Stewart has also cost the Reds on the basepaths. He takes an extra base on just 25% of opportunities, and he’s also made seven outs on the bases this year. Conversely, Wetherholt runs the bases like the leadoff hitter he is. He takes an extra base on 52% of his chances to do so, and he’s only made a single out on the bases this year. That’s an enormous gap. One way of thinking about it? Stewart has been on second base when his team hit a single 11 times this year. He stopped at third five times, scored five times, and got thrown out at home once. Wetherholt has been on second when his team hit a single 20 times this year; he’s stopped at third four times and scored 16 times.
That’s a lot of value that doesn’t show up in the box score. Specifically, if you assign run values to all of that based on how much advancing or making an out changes your team’s scoring expectation, Stewart has been 3.5 runs below average, while Wetherholt has been 1.8 runs above average. Between that and the gap in steals, there’s a seven-run gap in baserunning value between the two. Benge is even a hair better than Wetherholt on the bases, for the record. That passes the sniff test for me; on our leaderboards, Wetherholt and Benge are each one of the best 20 baserunners in baseball this year, while Stewart is one of the 20 worst. But baserunning just isn’t all that important – seven runs of difference is very little. Heck, Yordan Alvarez is a worse baserunner than Stewart and it just doesn’t matter.
The tale of the tape on offense looks like this:
| Metric | Stewart | Wetherholt | Benge |
|---|---|---|---|
| FG Off* | 8.1 | 5.3 | 13.1 |
| RE24 | 20.3 | 10.2 | 11.3 |
| BsR | -3.9 | 3.2 | 3.6 |
| WPA** | 1.35 | 1.99 | 0.53 |
**: denominated in wins, while all other stats are denominated in runs
I think it’s pretty clear that Stewart has been the better player on offense this year, and I think it’s reasonable to think that Benge has been roughly as good as him. I think it’s equally clear that the gap is fairly narrow. Stewart has gotten run-scoring opportunities and cashed them in adroitly. Wetherholt has been a smaller-scale success, but he’s also been good at his role. He leads off and gets on base. We like that, just like we like sluggers who send runners on the basepaths home to celebrate. Wetherholt is also getting it done on the basepaths, while Stewart isn’t. But even though Wetherholt has been one of the best baserunners in baseball and Stewart one of the worst, that gap is smaller than the difference in their production with the bat.
If we were only allowed to consider offensive value, I’d vote for Stewart over Wetherholt. I might vote for Benge over both of them. Considering how many different statistics I looked at that all landed in a similar place, I think the only fair read is that the three are fairly close. All three of these guys were assets to their team on offense, as I’m quite sure that fans of their teams would tell you. But defense matters too, and realistically, this one isn’t as close.
Now, it’s good to remember that defensive metrics are noisy and that you shouldn’t take them as gospel. It’s very hard to measure defensive talent. If someone quotes you an FRV number and tells you that it proves, beyond a doubt, how good a player was with the glove, you have my permission to make a fart noise with your mouth to show them how you feel about it. But let me make some gentle assertions and see what you think about them.
I assert that for the same offensive value, you’d prefer to have a second baseman compared to a first baseman. I don’t think this is particularly controversial. Jose Altuve and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. have very similar career batting lines. Regardless of how you feel about the banging scheme, does anyone think Vlad’s 132 wRC+ at first is more valuable than Altuve’s 127 wRC+ at second? Second basemen aren’t as good of hitters as first basemen! Big league first basemen have a 115 wRC+ this year; big league second basemen have a 95 wRC+ (right fielders are at a 102 wRC+).
The reason for that split is that there’s some minimum defensive level necessary to play second base, and a lot of first basemen don’t clear it. If they did, they’d go play second and improve their team’s offense by a huge amount. I don’t require you to convert that gap into some exact number of wins, but surely, you’ll concede the weak form of my argument – given the same results on offense, a second baseman is more valuable than a first baseman.
Okay, another assertion: JJ Wetherholt is a plus defensive second baseman. Again, I don’t think this is controversial. Every advanced metric says that he’s phenomenal out there. He made only two errors in more than 1,000 innings, the third-lowest mark out of 29 second basemen who played 500 or more innings. He notched 0.48 assists plus putouts per inning – outs per inning, roughly speaking. That’s fifth highest out of that group of 29. He was one of the best at making outs, and also one of the best at avoiding errors. He was first in double plays started per inning, though I’ll give some of that credit to Masyn Winn. He’s the best defensive second baseman by a mile according to Statcast’s FRV, and in the top five according to both DRS and Baseball Prospectus’ RDA. He passes the eye test. He’s the betting favorite to win the NL Gold Glove at second base. You don’t have to put a run value on it to say that Wetherholt has been an excellent fielder at an important defensive position.
One last assertion about defense: Sal Stewart is a middling defender. I’m not trying to say he’s bad. He played across the infield as a prospect, and the Reds have occasionally run him out at second and third this year, but they prefer to play him at first base. His versatility is occasionally valuable even now – he’s made four mid-game position switches in the last two months – but for the most part, he’s their everyday first baseman. That makes sense to me; that’s where our prospect team thought he’d end up, where scouts across the industry thought he’d end up, and where his team clearly thinks he’s the best fit.
I don’t believe the advanced metrics that say Stewart is a bad first base defender. It’s very hard to figure out defensive value at first base, and while Statcast thinks he’s below average at receiving throws, I’m not confident enough in their numbers, given the newness of the statistic and the few innings Stewart has played, to think he’s anything other than average. I bet he’ll improve over time, too; the Reds didn’t give him much playing time at first in the minors, so he’ll continue to learn on the job. But nevertheless, he’s not some defensive wizard out there.
That doesn’t matter all that much when it comes to my estimation of Stewart’s trajectory as a baseball player. He plays a position where they pay you to hit, and he hits. Sounds good to me. But you can have that in your head, and also say that on the defensive side of the ball, you’d prefer Wetherholt. Forget the magnitude for a minute – Gold Glove-contender second baseman or bat-first corner infielder looking for a defensive home. Leave their offense out of the comparison and weigh the two defensive profiles against each other, and there’s a clear winner.
Benge doesn’t fit quite as cleanly into the discussion here, so I left him for last. He’s a good right fielder, thanks in large part to his cannon arm; he’s thrown out 10 baserunners on the year. Generally speaking, I’d rather have an excellent second baseman than a good right fielder, but this is a closer call for me. To continue my analogizing to past Astros, I’d prefer Altuve (career 127 wRC+) to George Springer (career 128 wRC+). But defensive metrics are noisy, and if you thought Benge was just as good of a defender as Wetherholt, I’d disagree with you but wouldn’t think you were being unreasonable.
Where does that leave us? With a decision to make about how much we care about hitting, baserunning, and fielding. I can’t choose those weights for you. You might think that hitting is worth 30 times more than baserunning or fielding, or that baserunning is the most important by a mile. I think you’d be silly to think either, but your opinions are your own. I can, however, tell you my own views.
Of those three phases, hitting is the one I care about most. It’s the most stable, and you can stack up the most value there. Alvarez, the best hitter in baseball this year, checks in at 70 RE24. Crow-Armstrong, in one of the greatest defensive seasons of all time, is something like 25 runs above average in center. Witt is first in baseball in baserunning value, 8.5 runs above average. The ranges don’t lie.
But we’re not choosing between the best hitter in baseball and the best fielder in baseball. We’re choosing between a good-hitting first baseman, a solid-hitting second baseman who’s also a very good defender and baserunner, and a right fielder who does everything well. If Wetherholt were swinging a wet noodle out there, it wouldn’t matter how many double plays he turned or how many times he took the extra base. But heck, he got on base more frequently than Stewart this year in a tougher home park for offense, and he’s also approaching the 20-homer plateau. Benge is also right on the doorstep of 20 homers, and he’s similarly electric on the bases and no slouch in the field. They aren’t chopped liver.
For me, the decision is very close at the top – and it’s between Wetherholt and Benge. I’d put Stewart in third despite his enviable run production totals. I understand why Stewart is a leading contender despite WAR not liking his season. I think that people who say to completely ignore RBIs and batting average are missing the point. But I think that blindly taking RBI totals is just as bad as blindly taking WAR totals (worse, really, but both are bad). Context is important everywhere in life, and baseball is no exception. For me, the sum total of Wetherholt’s and Benge’s seasons across hitting, running, and fielding is better than Stewart’s in the same categories. I’d vote for Wetherholt, but I’ll level with you: I started this tale of the tape thinking it was a clear choice and ended it thinking that I’d be pretty happy voting for Benge too.
If you’re a voter reading this, I hope you take my advice into consideration and look at each candidate’s total contributions in context to make your decision. Like I said, I wouldn’t fault you for voting for Stewart if you think his performance at the plate is so staggering that the rest of it doesn’t matter. But if you’re just looking at the RBI total and going on that, I urge you to broaden your horizons just a little bit before making a choice. And if you’re a fan, well, there’s really no losing here. Any of these three would be deserving winners. I hope you enjoyed this comically long discussion of the most fascinating awards race of the season in any case.
Ben is a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @benclemens.

By now, you've probably seen Vladimir Guerrero Jr.'s comments about his 2026 season and his contract, right?
Let's just say it made the rounds in the media pretty quickly…
For those who haven't seen it, Vladdy said he's being paid for what he's done in the past, not for what he's going to do.
We talked about it on the Passion MLB podcast on Wednesday night.
@passion_mlb podcast with Pascal Harvey and @SebasBerrouard
Vladdy's comments, the Blue Jays' elimination, and the race for the playoffs are on the agenda https://t.co/4wwfQq6p9b
— Charles-Alexis Brisebois (@Charles__Alexis) September 24, 2026
Obviously, hearing Vladdy say things like that can really give the impression that he doesn't feel enough pressure to perform.
And after a disastrous season—in which he was a major reason the Blue Jays missed the playoffs—let's just say that seeing him shift the blame like this is upsetting to fans.
After Game 2 of yesterday's doubleheader, John Schneider was asked about the hot topic among Blue Jays fans.
And the manager, naturally, came to his player's defense.
John Schneider said that Vladdy's comments had “unfortunate timing,” but they will help him deal with “feeling the weight of being the guy every single day.”
“The player, the person I know in Vlad, is by no means saying, ‘OK, I got paid and I'm good with that.'” #BlueJays
— Keegan Matheson (@KeeganMatheson) September 24, 2026
Schneider spoke of “bad timing” and the fact that the club will help him manage the pressure of being the big name in town.
He added that his first baseman works hard and isn't the type to rest on his laurels just because he signed his contract.
John Schneider on Vlad Guerrero Jr.'s viral comments: “The
person I know—Vlad—is by no means saying, ‘Okay, I got paid and I'm good with that.' I know the kind of worker he is, the kind of player he is, the kind of teammate he is… he's going to continue to work to have a better year.”
— Hazel Mae (@thehazelmae) September 24, 2026
The truth is, I don't know if Schneider really means what he said. But he had no choice but to defend his player publicly.
That's the right thing to do in 2026.
I imagine, however, that Schneider and his bosses are going to have a serious talk with Vladdy about the significance of his contract and the expectations placed on him.
We thought it was clear, but apparently, some people need things explained to them more often than not.

first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. is batting .263 with nine home runs and 56 RBIs.
The 27-year-old is not having a good year. His .695 on-base plus slugging percentage trails his .840 career mark. His nine home runs this year match his total from the 60-game 2020 season, his worst total in a season so far.
The Blue Jays' postseason dreams ended on Wednesday. Knowing Toronto played all seven games of the World Series only last year makes this result even more disappointing.
It wasn't the only thing that enraged the fans Wednesday. Guerrero received massive criticism after clips of a Spanish-language interview went viral.
In the interview, Guerrero discussed his franchise-record extension, a 14-year, $500 million deal he signed in April 2025.
"They didn't pay me because I'm going to hit 40 every year," he told Dominican TV host Veronica Batista. He said the deal rewarded what he already did.
After Wednesday's loss, Guerrero said he does not regret the comments. But he also said he will prepare for next season and "keep working hard" in the offseason.
Amid the backlash, one more quote from him flew under the radar.
Vladimir Guerrero Opens Up About Unfortunate News
In the same interview, Guerrero said he has felt depression and anxiety at times this season.
"I've been dealing with a back injury all year," Guerrero said. "It's not a very serious injury. Some days I wake up feeling fine and other days I wake up in pain. But that's no excuse for the bad season I've had. I've felt depression and anxiety. There are times when I've called my dad late at night to open up to him."
Noticias Telemicro reported that Guerrero leans on his father, Hall of Famer Vladimir Guerrero, during anxious moments. Guerrero also said Wednesday that he thinks about his contract after every failed at-bat.
This is Guerrero's first season without Bo Bichette. The 28-year-old, his teammate since both debuted in 2019, signed with the New York Mets in January.
Sportsnet's Shi Davidi reported last week that Guerrero also asked manager John Schneider for help. The season has been weighing on his shoulders.
John Schneider Defends Vladimir Guerrero on Contract Comments
John Schneider on Vlad Guerrero Jr. viral comments:
“The person I know – Vlad – by no means is he saying ‘okay I got paid and I'm good with that,’ I know the type of worker he is, the player he is, type of teammate he is.. he's going to continue to work to have a better year.”
— Hazel Mae (@thehazelmae) September 24, 2026
Schneider said Wednesday that the comments had "unfortunate timing." He said the Blue Jays would help Guerrero handle the weight of being "the guy every single day."
Schneider rejected the idea that Guerrero feels satisfied because he got paid. "The person I know, Vlad, by no means is he saying, 'OK, I got paid and I'm good with that.'"
"I know the type of worker he is, the player he is, type of teammate he is," Schneider said. "He's going to continue to work to have a better year," he added.
Toronto closes its season with three home games against the Cincinnati Reds, starting Friday.

item.content:encoded:
We’re down to the final days of the 2026 regular season with still quite a number of teams that have something to play for -- including a few who are fighting for their postseason lives.
Such is the case with the Astros and Rangers, who are tied atop the AL West (with Houston owning the tiebreaker); the team that loses the division will most likely miss the playoffs entirely. Elsewhere in the American League, the Guardians and White Sox are still battling for the division title, though the loser of that should slot into the third wild-card spot.
While all the divisions in the National League have been clinched already, the wild-card race, specifically in terms of seeding, is very much heating up, with the Phillies, Cubs and Padres entering play on Wednesday in a three-way tie.
Which clubs will get to keep playing into October? And which will watch their playoff aspirations come to an end?
Our expert panel has ranked every team based on a combination of what we’ve seen so far and what we already knew going into the 162-game marathon that is a full baseball season. We also asked ESPN MLB experts Bradford Doolittle, Buster Olney and Jorge Castillo to weigh in with an observation for all 30 teams.
1. Milwaukee Brewers
Record: 99-59
Previous ranking: 1
With the season down to a handful of games, the Brewers have all but run out of time for Kyle Harrison to recover his first-half form. Harrison was 8-2 with a 3.01 ERA before the break; he’s 2-3 with a 7.80 ERA since. His strikeout rate has remained steady, even as his velocity and movement measures have become more volatile. Meanwhile, his walk rate has more than doubled, and his homers-allowed rate has nearly tripled. Suffice to say, this is not a great combination of trends. Milwaukee has tried to get Harrison back in stride by using him out of the bullpen, but he’s gotten hammered as a reliever. Brewers fans who dreamed of a big three rotation of Jacob Misiorowski, Harrison and Logan Henderson probably need to recalibrate their expectations at this point. -- Doolittle
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
Record: 97-61
Previous ranking: 2
We’re nearing October baseball, and it’s as if the Dodgers are knocking off items on a to-do list. Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup? Check. Edwin Diaz finding his stuff, finally? Check. Will Smith back in the lineup? Check -- and he has an OPS of close to 1.000 this month. Mookie Betts back to being Mookie Betts? Check. Kyle Tucker digging out of his seasonlong slump? Check. L.A. is putting the pieces back together just in time as it begins its effort to become the first NL team to go back-to-back-to-back. -- Olney
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Record: 96-62
Previous ranking: 3
Tampa Bay began the season with the longest odds to win the AL East. On Tuesday, it clinched its first division title since 2021 with a win over the Yankees. The Rays will enter their first postseason since 2023 as the favorites to win the AL pennant behind a distinct home-field advantage at Tropicana Field, a strong pitching staff and a dynamic lineup centered around MVP candidate Junior Caminero, designated hitter Yandy Diaz and first baseman Jonathan Aranda. With a payroll that ranks 28th in the majors, the Rays seek to become the team with the lowest-ranked payroll to ever win the World Series. -- Castillo
4. Atlanta Braves
Record: 93-65
Previous ranking: 5
Atlanta would’ve preferred to get a first-round bye in the playoffs, of course, but the fact that the Brewers and Dodgers seemed to have locked down the No. 1 and No. 2 seeds allows the Braves to treat this last week of the regular season like the last week of spring training. They can plot out the best way to rest their key relievers, assess the progress of Robert Suarez and arrange at-bats for the position players to be primed for the postseason. Meanwhile, the teams the Braves are likely to face in the first round -- the Phillies, Cubs and Padres -- are all still pushing for berths and home-field advantage in the wild-card round. -- Olney
5. New York Yankees
Record: 91-67
Previous ranking: 4
Despite manager Aaron Boone saying on Tuesday that Aaron Judge isn’t expected to return from his calf strain in time for the wild-card round, Judge told ESPN the following day that he does in fact intend to be ready for Game 1. He suffered the injury last Wednesday and was placed on the injured list two days later. The Yankees were initially cryptic about the setback, declining to disclose the severity and Judge’s outlook.
Boone offered some clarity Tuesday when he called it a “moderate strain” and acknowledged that the club does not plan on having him to open the postseason. Judge received a PPP injection Monday. The Yankees hope that will spur recovery. Otherwise, New York faces an uphill challenge to survive in October without its three-time MVP at his best. -- Castillo
6. Chicago Cubs
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 6
No player has made more of a second-half leap than Alex Bregman, whose season has just gathered momentum almost daily since the last week of July. That momentum was stopped in its tracks when Bregman suffered facial fractures last weekend when struck by a foul ball. The good news is that the Cubs decided against placing Bregman on the IL, believing he might be ready for the playoffs after.
But even if that proves to be optimistic, Cubs fans can take solace in the presence of icy-cool rookie Pedro Ramirez. The Cubs didn’t drop off much when Dansby Swanson was injured, as Ramirez provided a league-average bat and glove work at both second and third base that has kept an elite Cubs defense on track. You want Bregman in there, for sure -- but Ramirez provides a heck of a Plan B. -- Doolittle
7. San Diego Padres
Record: 88-70
Previous ranking: 8
San Diego’s magic number for clinching a playoff spot is shrinking, allowing general manager A.J. Preller and skipper Craig Stammen the chance to line up their staff for the wild-card series, with options developing. Stammen indicated to reporters that unless Michael King is needed to clinch a playoff spot on the last day of the regular season, he will be held over to start Game 1 of the wild card, wherever that is -- so he wouldn’t necessarily be used Sunday in order to win home-field advantage in the first round of the playoffs.
Additionally, the Padres are in a better position to rest their bullpen, the perceived strength of the team. Adrian Morejon ranks third among all relievers in innings. Rest might be overrated for Mason Miller: He has made 16 appearances on zero days’ rest, and in those games, he has allowed two hits and one earned run in 16⅔ innings, with two walks and 27 strikeouts. -- Olney
8. Philadelphia Phillies
Record: 87-71
Previous ranking: 7
The culture of Philadelphia’s starting pitchers, from Zack Wheeler to Cristopher Sanchez to Aaron Nola, is to pitch deep into games. Unlike so many starters in this generation, Wheeler takes the mound expecting to work into the late innings -- and the Phillies will need this sort of production from the rotation, given the team’s recent bullpen problems. Orion Kerkering, an important part of the relief corps, struggled so badly that he was sent to the minors last week. Jose Alvarado has pitched better down the stretch, and hard-throwing Alex MacFarlane has quickly ascended into an important role in his rookie season in the bullpen. But the Phillies’ rotation will carry the team’s October dreams. -- Olney
9. Boston Red Sox
Record: 85-73
Previous ranking: 9
The Red Sox rewarded Chad Tracy on Tuesday for leading the team’s historic turnaround by removing his interim tag and giving him a three-year contract to continue as manager. Now he’ll look to accomplish what his predecessor Alex Cora couldn’t last year: beating the Yankees on the road in the AL Wild Card Series.
Boston has cooled off since going 32-5 to put itself in playoff position and faces some injury uncertainty going into October. Ceddanne Rafaela returned Tuesday after missing 16 games with a quad injury, and Willson Contreras was hit by a pitch on his right hand last Thursday and is dealing with soreness. On the mound, the Red Sox could receive two significant reinforcements for the bullpen in Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck. Crochet, last season’s AL Cy Young runner-up, has been out with a shoulder injury since late April, while Houck hasn’t appeared in a game in 2026. -- Castillo
10. Cleveland Guardians
Record: 82-76
Previous ranking: 12
Cleveland is, once again, showing its knack for a strong finishing kick. Over the past decade, only the Dodgers have won more September games. For Guardians fans aching for their team’s first title since the Truman administration, October is a higher priority at this point.
Like the White Sox, the first order of business is to secure the AL Central title and the first-round bye likely to go with it. Given the neck-and-neck nature of Cleveland’s battle with Chicago, there likely isn’t going to be much time for manager Stephen Vogt to ease up on the pedal to finish the season. That would be nice to do when it comes to rookie ace Parker Messick, who will finish the season with at least 50 more innings than he has ever thrown in a season. Messick has shown no signs of fatigue, so it may not matter. -- Doolittle
11. Arizona Diamondbacks
Record: 84-74
Previous ranking: 10
Manager Torey Lovullo’s comments in a radio interview last week in which he acknowledged that the Diamondbacks “probably” -- his word -- need to reach the postseason to earn him a contract extension surprised many in the industry, as Lovullo has a strong and long-standing relationship with his boss, Mike Hazen. The Ketel Marte situation has been challenging for the organization, with the team’s highest-paid position player failing to show up to the park, and owner Ken Kendrick has a reputation for being mercurial and demanding. Lovullo’s contract runs out at season’s end, and he and the Diamondbacks agreed they would discuss his status then. -- Olney
12. Chicago White Sox
Record: 81-77
Previous ranking: 11
The White Sox have wobbled down the stretch, but they have not fallen down. It looks like they will join the playoff party, completing an incredible two-year turnaround that saw them go from setting the modern single-season loss record to playing in October.
Barring a face-plant over the last few days of the season, the question of whether the Sox can overtake Cleveland for the AL Central title is the biggest remaining question. It’s impactful, with a first-round bye likely on the line. A bye is a boon for any team, but among likely postseason entrants, it might loom largest for the White Sox. That’s just because of how manager Will Venable has had to stretch his pitching resources to the maximum just to get to this point. A wild-card skip would give his staff at least a little time to regroup before the ALDS begins. -- Doolittle
13. Pittsburgh Pirates
Record: 80-78
Previous ranking: 14
Why did Paul Skenes lapse into baseball’s pitching middle class rather than continue his march toward Cooperstown? There is no bigger task for the Pirates and Skenes this offseason than figuring this out. With one more start to go, he has already allowed more runs this season than he did in his first two seasons combined. To be sure, it’s not all on Skenes, whose expected ERA, 3.27 per Statcast, is unusually divergent from his actual ERA (3.91). Still, even a 3.27 ERA is a far cry from the level of effectiveness Skenes flashed before this season. Why? Finding the answer to that question could prove to be the biggest addition Pittsburgh makes this winter. -- Doolittle
14. Texas Rangers
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 16
With eyes on the disappointing Mariners and Yordan Alvarez’s Triple Crown watch, the Rangers quietly remained in contention in the historically dreadful AL West all summer. Following three straight losses, they now find themselves tied atop the division with Houston. Texas will host the Mets in a series finale Thursday before finishing the season with three games in Minnesota. The Rangers will need to finish with a better record than the Astros, who own the tiebreaker, to reach the postseason for the first time since winning the 2023 World Series. -- Castillo
15. Houston Astros
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 13
The Astros fired general manager Dana Brown last month and are under .500 with four games remaining ... but they still have a real chance to win the division. That’s the AL West in 2026. The Astros finish the regular season with a four-game series in West Sacramento against an A’s team that has an MLB-worst run differential. The bad news: The Astros head there tied atop the division. The good news: They hold the tiebreaker over Texas. In the background over the last few days of the season: Alvarez’s push to become the first player to win a Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2013. -- Castillo
16. Toronto Blue Jays
Record: 77-82
Previous ranking: 15
The Blue Jays did not replicate their 2025 magic in 2026, largely due to injuries and their offense falling off a cliff. They finished last season fourth in the majors with a 112 wRC+; this season, they’re tied for 24th with a 95 wRC+. The dropoff starts with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and George Springer. Guerrero has nine home runs -- and, inexplicably, just one at home -- with a .695 OPS in the first year of a 14-year, $500 million contract extension. Springer, who reversed a precipitous decline to hit 32 home runs with a .959 OPS last season, has 15 home runs with a .730 OPS in 124 games this year -- and he’s a free agent after this season. Whether Springer re-signs or not, a rebound in 2027 starts with Guerrero sparking an offense that is tied for last in home runs in 2026. -- Castillo
17. Miami Marlins
Record: 78-80
Previous ranking: 18
Here’s the good news about the Marlins’ 2026 season: They hung around all year, battling among the contenders and having some individual successes. Here’s what’s not-so-great about where they stand right now: It’s hard to identify the players who could lead a Miami breakout into full-scale contention with the best NL teams.
Otto Lopez had an excellent season, but he’ll turn 28 years old next week and his OPS is under .800. Griffin Conine is the one player on the team with an OPS over .800, and he’s 29. Sandy Alcantara reestablished himself as a rotation leader, but he’s 31. Eury Perez has flashes of dominance and is just 23, but he’s got an injury history and will finish this season with an ERA over 4.00. More depth and more talent is needed for the Marlins to take the next step. -- Olney
18. Baltimore Orioles
Record: 78-81
Previous ranking: 19
Another disappointing season in Baltimore has already prompted some changes in the front office, but not at the top. President of baseball operations Mike Elias is expected to return in 2027. One move his front office got right was signing Pete Alonso last winter. The first baseman, who has played in every game this season, hit his 40th home run of the season in Monday’s win over the Blue Jays. He clearly isn’t why the Orioles aren’t going to the postseason for the second straight year.
Baltimore’s young position player core has not lived up to the hype, while the pitching staff wasn’t good enough to shoulder the load. Elias & Co. already decided to move on from former No. 1 pick Adley Rutschman, an All-Star catcher previously considered a foundational player, at the trade deadline. More significant moves could come this offseason. -- Castillo
19. St. Louis Cardinals
Record: 77-81
Previous ranking: 17
This rebuilding season has been an unqualified success for the Cardinals. If not for a leaky bullpen, their soft wild-card contention might have been a lot more solid. While bullpens are sometimes the final piece of the contention puzzle for a building team, that’s not always the case. Some clubs develop a bullpen-building process that takes effect even as the rest of the roster remains a work in progress. The Pirates of recent vintage are a good example.
Thus, the project of putting together a contention-worthy bullpen is a crucial one for the Chaim Bloom-led front office. Bloom was part of a Rays front office that annually churned out elite, no-name bullpens. However, during the four years that Bloom led the Red Sox front office, Boston ranked 24th in bullpen ERA (4.48) and middle-of-the-pack in save percentage. Good first year, but there is more to prove in St. Louis. -- Doolittle
20. Detroit Tigers
Record: 74-85
Previous ranking: 20
The Tigers will probably finish fourth in the AL in run differential, perhaps third if they pass the Red Sox, and will easily pace the Central by that measure. When you consider that, along with Detroit’s freakishly bad record in one- and two-run games (now 21-51) and the relatively short list of players on expiring deals (Jack Flaherty and Gleyber Torres, along with the retiring Justin Verlander), the Tigers are an obvious and very strong bounce-back candidate for the 2027 season. That doesn’t mean that president of baseball operations Scott Harris and his staff don’t have their work cut out for them when it comes to evaluating this lackluster season. Still, for the Tigers’ disappointed fans, it’s important to keep in mind that their team will be proceeding from a relative position of strength. -- Doolittle
21. Washington Nationals
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 23
In so many ways, the 2026 season was a success for the Nationals, who exceeded expectations this year, flirting with contention in the first half and seeing the development of players like CJ Abrams and James Wood into offensive stars. But the team’s pitching collapsed in the second half -- Washington’s second-half ERA of 4.49 ranks 25th. The Nationals locked down Cade Cavalli to a multiyear deal last week at the end of what has been a breakout season, but it’s clear that president of baseball operations Paul Toboni’s greatest challenge is to develop the sort of pipeline of pitching that will allow them to compete with the big-market teams in the division. -- Olney
22. Seattle Mariners
Record: 74-84
Previous ranking: 24
A year after falling one win short of the franchise’s first World Series appearance, the Mariners’ season will end Sunday with a whimper. The 2026 campaign will be remembered as the most disappointing one in franchise history.
Cal Raleigh’s drop-off from 60 home runs and an MVP runner-up finish was baffling. Julio Rodriguez regressed and still hasn’t made the superstar jump widely expected of him. Josh Naylor was a below-average hitter in the first year of his five-year contract. The starting rotation was not as good as advertised. Changes are inevitable, likely starting with manager Dan Wilson. But the Mariners can’t fire all of their players. They’ll need their core to bounce back from down seasons in order to rebound in 2027. -- Castillo
23. New York Mets
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 21
No one will go into the 2027 season under more pressure than David Stearns, the Mets’ head of baseball operations, following their collapse down the stretch in 2025 and the poor 2026 season. So it makes sense that he worked to keep someone he has a working relationship with in the managerial role, Andy Green, who had his interim tag removed and was hired to a three-year deal Tuesday. Steve Cohen’s comments on an SNY broadcast about needing new voices within the organization got the attention of a lot of rival executives, who wondered if the impact of Pete Alonso’s encore performance at Citi Field and the “Fire Stearns” chants last week made an impression on the owner. Under the circumstances, hiring Green seems like the right move for Stearns, the smart move. -- Olney
24. Minnesota Twins
Record: 75-84
Previous ranking: 22
The arrival of prospects Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins and Emmanuel Rodriguez has the Twins’ prospective 2027 position group in good shape even if veteran Josh Bell declines his mutual option and departs. The murkiest position is catcher, where Ryan Jeffers is likely headed for free agency, presumably after the Twins issue him a qualifying offer. The QO could limit Jeffers’ market, but probably not that much, as Jeffers looks like the best free agent catcher option out there. If he leaves, the Twins will need someone to pair with Caratini.
Long term, after drafting Vahn Lackey third in the most recent draft, the Twins seem in good shape with him, Eduardo Tait, Khadim Diaw and Carson Tinney all showing well in prospect rankings. Alas, none of that quartet is likely to be a 2027 solution. -- Doolittle
25. Cincinnati Reds
Record: 73-85
Previous ranking: 25
The ongoing maturation of Elly De La Cruz, as he edges toward his career prime, has provided ample reason to keep an eye on the Reds, even amid a last-place showing. Still, there have been enough trade rumors regarding the supremely talented shortstop to make you wonder just how long De La Cruz will be around.
Recent comments made by his agent, Scott Boras, don’t help. Boras suggested to reporters that a future foray into the open market made more sense for De La Cruz than a below-market extension. What does that mean for the Reds in the near term? For now, he has three more years of team control, so there’s no reason to be rash. Still, with this cloud starting to form over Great American Park, some sort of clarity about how the Reds plan to deal with their best player would be nice. -- Doolittle
26. Kansas City Royals
Record: 68-90
Previous ranking: 26
The Royals’ biggest offseason project will be to figure out their 2027 bullpen formula. That process begins with evaluating the relievers already on hand. Presumed closer Carlos Estevez had shoulder surgery -- bafflingly not until the second week of September -- and the Royals almost certainly won’t pick up their 2027 club option on him. Lucas Erceg looked lost before being shipped off to Omaha, but he performed well in Triple-A and his velocity upon his return to the majors has been at its highest level all year. Which Erceg is the real one? Is journeyman righty Nate Pearson a leverage option? Does Craig Kimbrel have anything left? The Royals will need relief help from outside the organization, but how much of it will depend on the outcome of these evaluations and others. -- Doolittle
27. San Francisco Giants
Record: 65-94
Previous ranking: 27
The general perception of San Francisco’s farm system is that it improved in 2026, and Bryce Eldridge established himself as a player the organization could build around. Beyond that, however, the Giants really haven’t progressed. They have a top-heavy payroll situation, with hundreds of millions owed to Rafael Devers, Willy Adames and Matt Chapman. The questions about manager Tony Vitello making the jump from college to professional baseball weren’t quelled by his first season with the Giants -- and neither were the questions about the man who hired him, Buster Posey, who is still relatively new to his front office role. -- Olney
28. Athletics
Record: 63-95
Previous ranking: 28
The A’s are stumbling to the finish line having lost 95 games. All-Star catcher Shea Langeliers recently returned from knee surgery, but several other prominent players remain on the IL, including Nick Kurtz, Tyler Soderstrom, Jacob Wilson, Brent Rooker, Luis Severino and Gage Jump. They’ll enter their season-ending series against the Astros with a negative-217 run differential -- the worst in the majors by 33 runs. With one season remaining before the A’s move to Las Vegas in 2028, they enter the winter in search of a general manager after David Forst’s departure in early August. Their offseason priorities are straightforward: Get healthy and improve a pitching staff that has a 5.43 ERA (29th) despite pitching half its games at the launchpad known as Sutter Health Park. -- Castillo
29. Los Angeles Angels
Record: 60-98
Previous ranking: 29
The Angels, despite 11 straight losing seasons, are the only franchise in the majors that has yet to post a 100-loss season. That could change this weekend in Seattle, where the Angels will need to win three of four games to avoid reaching the century mark. It’d be a fitting conclusion to Arte Moreno’s tenure as owner. Last month, Moreno agreed to sell controlling interest in the team to Stan Kroenke for a record valuation of $4 billion. Kroenke will take over a franchise that has not appeared in the postseason since 2014 and has not won a postseason game since 2009.
The first order of business this offseason will be hiring fired general manager Perry Minasian’s replacement. The team could also be in search of a manager to replace Kurt Suzuki, who is on a one-year contract. It is a transformative time in Anaheim. -- Castillo
30. Colorado Rockies
Record: 57-101
Previous ranking: 30
Colorado has compiled 100 losses for the fourth consecutive season; the last team to suffer 100-plus losses in five consecutive seasons were the Phillies, from 1938 to 1942. In Paul DePodesta’s first year of running Colorado’s baseball operations, there were some under-the-hood improvements: the biggest run differential improvement of all 30 teams in 2026, an improved farm system and some nice finds for the every-day lineup, like Jake McCarthy, TJ Rumfield and Connor Norby. There’s still a long way to go to competitive relevance for the Rockies, especially given the high bar required in the Dodgers’ NL West. -- Olney

item.content:encoded:
Vladimir Guerrero Jr. raised some eyebrows earlier this week when he talked about his struggles at the plate this season. In a Spanish language interview with Veronica Batista, the Toronto Blue Jays star explained that he doesn't get paid to hit 40 home runs every year because he is being paid for what he already accomplished.
He has hit nine home runs in 142 games this season. That is the same amount he hit in 60 games during the COVID-shortened 2020 season.
Guerrero signed a 14-year, $500 million contract with the Blue Jays ahead of the 2025 season. He only hit 23 home runs during the regular season last year. However he did step it up in the postseason. He won ALCS MVP and hit eight home runs as he helped carry Toronto to the World Series for the first time this century. In Guerrero's eyes, that more than justifies the half-billion. Via MLB.com:
"I want people to understand one thing," Guerrero said in Spanish. "The money they gave me wasn't for what I'm going to do. It was for what I already did. They didn't pay me because I'm going to hit 40 every year. They paid me for what I already accomplished. People are confused about that, but I think the same way they do. Like, sometimes I even say to myself: bro, they gave you all that money and you're out here doing nothing. I try."
Interestingly enough, Guererro has only hit 40 home runs once in eight seasons when he had 48 to lead the American League in 2021. Other than that he's only hit 30 twice with 32 being the closest he's gotten to 40 since. It's not hard to see why so many people did a double take when they saw Guerrero's quote.
Vladdy defends comments, work ethic
Sep 2, 2026; Cleveland, Ohio, USA; Toronto Blue Jays first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. (27) rounds the bases after hitting a three-run home run during the second inning against the Cleveland Guardians at Progressive Field. Mandatory Credit: Ken Blaze-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
Guerrero was asked about it on Wednesday and did not back down. Via MLB.com:
"That was a quote from the interview when she asked me how I felt about this year. I said that, obviously, I feel really bad about the year that I had, that I couldn't help my team get to the postseason. I said I felt that it's my personal opinion, that every player gets paid for what they have done."
He then pointed out that his big postseason last year came after he signed the new deal. And more importantly, said he has never stopped working hard. He makes some good points and with the way professional sports restrict salaries for young players, there is often a case to be made that players are often paid as a reward for past performance, but that only happens when the team thinks they'll continue performing at an elite level.
So while Guerrero might be right, fans are not going to care if he doesn't produce. He still has a dozen years remaining on his contract. He's not going to find sympathy if he's struggling in the 2030's because the team almost won the World Series in 2025 and hit 48 home runs a year before that.

item.content:encoded:
Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has four games left before he can put his 2026 Toronto Blue Jays season behind him.
Guerrero, the six-time All-Star who signed the third highest-paid extension in MLB history in April 2025 at $500 million, has hit just nine home runs and slugged .359 to date for a career-low .695 OPS to date.
The Blue Jays, winners of the American League pennant this past season, where Guerrero was a major factor in reaching the World Series, were mathematically eliminated from this year’s postseason race as they hold a 77-81 record entering Wednesday.
